questions.q: The resistance of a wire is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi></math>. Its new resistance in ohm, if stretched to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>5</mn></math> times of its original length will be :
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
The resistance of a wire (R) is related to its resistivity ρ, length(l)  and cross-sectional area A as:

R=ρlA

As the length of wire increases, the cross-sectional area decreases. The cross-sectional area in terms of volume (V) and length (l) is

A=Vl

∴ R=ρl2V

Taking the volume of wire constant,

R∝l2

So if R' is the resistance of wire after getting redrawn and R is the initial resistance of wire,

∴ R'R=(5l)2l2=25⇒R'=25×R=125 Ω

Since, is=ip⇒2ε2r+2=2ε4+r⇒r=2 Ω

questions.q: The battery of a mobile phone is rated as 4.2 V , 5800 mAh. How much energy is stored in it when fully charged ?

questions.solution:
Given $\mathrm{V}=4.2$ volt

questions.q: A battery of <math><mrow><mn>3.0</mn><mtext> V</mtext></mrow></math> is connected to a resistor dissipating <math><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mtext> W</mtext></mrow></math> of power. If the terminal voltage of the battery is <math><mrow><mn>2.5</mn><mtext> V</mtext></mrow></math>, the power dissipated within the internal resistance is:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Given,

Emf of the battery, E=3 V

Potential difference across resister R is VR=2.5 V

Power dissipation in the resister is P=0.5 W

By using Kirchhoff's voltage law is given by,

Vr+VR=E  ...(1)

Vr is voltage across internal resister.

Using equation (1) and substitute the given values,

⇒Vr+2.5=3

⇒Vr=0.5

Now the ratio of potential across R and r is given by,

VRVr=IRIr=2.50.5=5

⇒Rr=5

Now the power dissipation across the internal resistance is given by

PRPr=I2RI2r=Rr

⇒PRPr=5

⇒Pr=PR5

⇒Pr=0.55=0.1W

questions.q: A <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math> long wire is broken into two unequal parts <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>X</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Y</mi></math>. The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>X</mi></math> part of the wire is stretched into another wire <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>W</mi></math>. Length of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>W</mi></math> is twice the length of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>X</mi></math> and the resistance of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>W</mi></math> is twice that of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Y</mi></math>. Find the ratio of length of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>X</mi></math> and<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Y</mi></math>.
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
​​​​​​​

Resistance of a wire is given by R=ρLA, where, ρ is conductivity, L is length of wire and A is cross-sectional area of wire.

For a single wire, A and ρ are constant.

Thus, for parts X and Y, resistance, RXRY=lXlY.

When wire is stretched to double of its length, then resistance becomes four times, thus, RW=4RX=2RY.

Hence, the ratio is RXRY=12.

So, lXlY=12
